title: LLM Programming and Theory Building
author: surprisetalk

excerpt: Last newsletter I was unhappy with my Tasktron workflow harness: The explicit state machine and reified effect design worked, but it obscured the core workflow, the harness’s raison d'être. I embarked on a rewrite, hoping to find a more concise and self-evident design based on durable effects (memoized steps) instead — something that would let the code express the intended behavior directly (“Do X, then do Y, then Z”) while being robust to crashes and transparently replayable. However, multiple weeks of attempts with Astra 6, Opus 5.5, and the newly released Sol 6.1 brought me no closer to the improved design I felt certain could exist. Despite my best efforts and instruction, I couldn’t get the models to emit tight, concise code; instead, they kept: This got me thinking about the two very different things I want from programming. The first thing is, well, just a program — something I run which does a straightforward task for me. Vibe-coding with LLMs has been great for these; I’m sure the models get up to all the nonsense I just mentioned, but it doesn’t matter to me — I’m not reading the code, I just want to dictate to my computer instead of typing, export from Photos.app, flash microcontrollers over the network, or a gazillion other things I haven’t bothered to publish because it’s hyper-specific software like mapping MIDI dials to my speaker volume and monitor brightness. I imagine this is what most people want from LLMs (and computers more broadly): Just solve some problem without making me care about the details. However, the second thing I want from programming is, just sometimes, to care about the details. I want a precise language and semantics to model something; to build up a theory. Sure, that theory should be useful for solving the immediate problem — but after that it’s also useful for thinking new thoughts.
